sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise par Rachel Hardiman, publiee sur paradoxography.org (site "Paradoxography", section Paradoxographus Vaticanus), consultee le 2026-08-20. IMPORTANT - licence : CC BY-SA 4.0 (partage a l'identique), differente du CC BY 4.0 du reste du corpus Zoomathia (meme situation que le fichier anglais d'Apollonius, zoo5/1e.xml). Selection : seuls les chapitres a contenu zoologique de l'oeuvre ont ete retenus (chapitres 1 a 9 sur les 62 que compte la traduction complete : grues, bete krokotta, respiration des animaux, animaux sans sang, poissons sans oesophage, cotes des serpents, os de lion, tortues du Gange). Le reste de l'oeuvre (a partir du chapitre 10) melange phenomenes hydrographiques et coutumes ethnographiques, non retenu ici. ATTENTION - appariement : la numerotation suit celle de la traduction consultee et ne correspond pas terme a terme a celle de l'edition grecque imprimee de Rohde utilisee pour le fichier '1g.xml' de ce dossier.

div.p: 1[1] Hagesias of Megara says that the cranes, whenever they are about to fly away from Thrace, are all sprinkled in purification in a circle by one of their number: then, when that one cries out, they rise up from the ground as if at the command of a boatswain, while the one that purifies them remains there. [2] Whenever they fly over the sea, two of them stretch out their wings, while one that has become tired rests by settling on them.

2 Dalion says, in Book 1 of his Aithiopika, that there is a beast in Ethiopia called the krokotta; when it approaches farmsteads, it eavesdrops upon those who are chatting, in particular on the names of the children. Coming by night, it speaks the names and, when the children come out, they are devoured by it.
3 Polites says that the young tuna (pelamys) in the Euxine Sea are generated from mud (pelos), and he says that they get their name because of this.

4[1] Aristotle says in his works on animals that all land animals that have lungs breathe, but that the wasp and bee do not breathe. [2](5) Those that have bladders also have intestines, but not all that have intestines have bladders.
5(6) Many animals are bloodless, but in general those that have more than four feet.
6(7) Fish do not have a gullet: because of this, the stomach of larger fish falls forward into their mouths when they chase smaller ones.
7(8)[1] Snakes have thirty ribs. [2] And if one pricks their eyes out, they grow back again, just like those of the swallow.
8(9) The bones of lions are so hard that when struck they often kindle fire.
9(10)[1] Polycleitus says that tortoises are found even in the Ganges, whose shells can hold five medimnoi. [2] Agatharchides [says] that they use †many† shells to roof their huts.
